title: From discs to tape and overdubbing
summary: Recording technology and its effect on pay.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: What do you think -- just to get back to some of the things -- let's take a break for a second.

Well, Jimmy, I want to ask you something about the future of music, what are you thinking about? Your thinking is most certainly along the same lines as mine. Where are the young musicians going and the future of music? Now, you and I came in -- you mentioned where we made discs and you'd better not make a mistake because if you did, you'd have to do that whole thing over again, which made some pretty good playing (inaudible) and percussion.
Then we got into tape where they could splice. And then we went from tape to --
They can take one note out.
Yeah, they can take one note out.
And you can go -- put in a mike, you just go "peep" and put it in.

Then we've got something now we call overdubbing, which has done us a great deal of harm, to my way of thinking, where you can come in and a whole band can do a piece on tape, then you can come in and bring some singers and some strings, and overdub on top of what's already been done.

Well, that's another thing that happened to us economically. Because you remember, they did that in the beginning, but the rule was that they had to pay the musicians. At first that used to prolong the dates because generally the star made more mistakes or was more fussy than anybody, and you'd make a million takes with the star. So it was kind of good when we had that overdubbing, most musicians were glad because the rule was that all the time they were tracking, or whatever you call it, we had to be paid. But unfortunately, we didn't have a monitor there so it kept getting smaller and smaller. So finally the union, to get off the hook about sending somebody around to keep checking on what they were doing, they said they had to pay you a minimum of one hour. And I don't think that rule even applies any more. You can just go in for 15 minutes, you get paid for 15 minutes. Then they
can submit a track and overdub for 12 hours, and you don't get anything more out of it.
So again, it's a fault, I'd say membership fault. I blame the union, like that's some mysterious thing. But we're the union, so it's a membership fault.
